processing: A cultivar, used for pan-fired Longjing and for baked famous greens; processing follows the style being made.
harvest_season: Early spring: buds usually break in early to mid March, some 3 to 5 days ahead of Longjing 43, so it reaches the market among the first teas of the year.
appearance_dry: When made as Longjing, flat, smooth, green leaves in the usual shape of that tea.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale green-yellow, as is typical of a fresh early green.
appearance_wet: Tender, even green buds and leaves, typical of an early-picked green.
taste_profile: Noted for a clear orchid fragrance over a fresh, sweet, gently savoury green base.

brewing.notes: Keep the water cool enough that the orchid note survives; a hotter steep flattens it.

vintage_note: Sold in the current spring only, and among the earliest of the season because of its early budding. Often labelled simply Longjing, or Longjing with the cultivar added by the seller. An early date on the pack is normal for this plant and does not by itself prove a higher grade.
description:
Zhongcha 108 is a modern tea plant, not a traditional tea: a cultivar from China's national tea institute in Hangzhou, derived from Longjing 43. Its appeal to growers and drinkers is simple. It buds early and it smells of orchids.

It was made for the Longjing method and takes it well, and it also works for baked famous greens. Growers like its strong budding, its long stay tender and its resistance to anthracnose, a common leaf disease.

Hand-finished Longjing from this cultivar is especially praised for its orchid aroma. Beyond that it tastes like a fresh early green: sweet, gentle and a little savoury. Keep the water around 80 C and short on leaf.

Not every seller names the cultivar, so ask. An early spring date is part of what this plant does, so ask about the area and picking as well as the date. Trying it next to Longjing 43 shows clearly what breeding changes.
history: The Tea Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences bred it from the irradiated offspring of Longjing 43, picking out a single plant; one trade account gives the period as 1986 to 2010. Researchers since then have tried it well beyond Zhejiang, including green tea trials against other cultivars, and Hangzhou's West Lake Longjing group standard names it among parent lines for breeding.
